newsitem.title: CHILE: Studies for Argentina-Chile mining treaty proceed.
newsitem.headline: Studies for Argentina-Chile mining treaty proceed.

text.p: Argentine and Chilean negotiators are about two months away from wrapping up technical studies for an agreement on mining cooperation, but the finished treaty could take much longer, Mining Minister Benjamin Teplizky said.

Teplizky said the treaty, aimed at promoting and regulating mining along their long border, has taken longer to negotiate than expected due to disagreements on various technical issues, including over how much territory the treaty should cover.
The Argentines want it to cover a larger area extending from the border than do the Chileans, he said.
"This negotiation has taken six years so far. It's an extremely complicated process, sorting out the technical, juridical, geological and political considerations," he told Reuters.
Negotiations are complicated by the fact that in Argentina, both national and provincial laws have to be reconciled, whereas in Chile only national laws apply.
He said he had no date for when the treaty might be finished but that inter-ministerial technical committees, comprised of officials from both countries, were making progress in setting basic terms.
"The technical studies should be finished in about 30 to 60 days, and from there it goes to the Foreign Ministry for studies," he said. "It's not easy and it's going to take a while."

Negotiations have taken so long that the two countries have drawn up protocols allowing mining companies to carry out metals prospecting on the border before the treaty is finished, Teplizky said. As an example, he cited two protocols allowing the El Pachon copper project and Pascua Lama gold mine to start work.
El Pachon is on the Argentine side of the border and Pascua Lama is a stone's throw away on the Chilean side.

The protocols, which went into effect in March, are officially considered the 19th and 20th addenda to a bilateral treaty on economic cooperation, signed by the governments of both countries in 1991. The protocols gave the green light to El Pachon, owned 50 percent by Canada's Cambior Inc and Pascua Lama gold prospect, being explored by Barrick Gold Corp.
